title: Steam's slower gate, agents' shorter memory
dek: Steam's review queue now runs up to 12 business days, and Valve has published what it checks. On the agent side, two studies say the same thing: give each task its own short context.

theme.mood: a Thursday about queues, checklists and keeping context small

tldr.text: Steam build review is taking up to **12 business days**, against a 3 to 5 day target. Valve's new release checklist says what to fix before you submit.
UK regulators banned mobile game ads that showed gameplay the games do not have, and a "not actual gameplay" label did not save them.
Coding agents lost about 12 points on average when made to juggle unfinished tasks in one session. A per-task state note won most of it back.
A 65B open-weight coding model claims to match models eight to fifteen times its size, on its maker's own benchmark run.
Safari's new beta can recolor light websites dark unless they declare a color scheme, and Cloudflare D1 now rejects query results over 50 MB.

blocks.title: Steam review now takes up to 12 days
blocks.gist: Valve says checking a game before release on Steam now takes up to 12 working days instead of 3 to 5, because far more games are being submitted. Most of the delay is games that fail and must be checked again.
blocks.background: Before a game can launch on Steam, Valve's team installs the build, plays it and checks it against the store page. A game that fails goes back into the queue after it is fixed.
body: In a Steamworks post on November 3, Valve said submissions for store page and build review rose sharply in recent months. It aims to test each build within 3 to 5 business days but is **taking up to 12** right now, and says much of that is re-reviewing games that failed on basic problems.

Its answer is a longer release checklist that catches those problems before submission: the game must have been played through Steam for 5 minutes, redistributables must be declared, achievements and cloud saves are checked, and the submit dialog now asks about every feature and language the store page promises.

Developers told Kotaku they waited two to three weeks without hearing back, and some missed launch dates. One game was rejected because reviewers could not find its local co-op, which uses two players on one keyboard.

Valve also listed what reviewers look for: a clear, complete store page with a legible logo, and a build that matches what the page promises, including content survey answers about mature content and AI use.

stat.label: business days a build review can take now, against a 3 to 5 day target

image.alt: Steamworks dialog "Mark build ready for review": checkboxes for testing through Steam on another PC, reviewer access to all content, and every store page feature present in the build.

terms.def: A packaged, runnable version of a game that is uploaded for testing or release.
Shared system libraries, such as DirectX or the Visual C++ runtime, that a game needs installed to run.
Steam's questionnaire where developers declare things like mature content and the use of AI in their game.

deep: The FAQ answer reads: typically within 3 to 5 business days, currently up to 12. Valve says more changes to build review are coming and that its release checklist documentation will be expanded; no date was given for queues returning to normal.

The new submit dialog is dynamic: it lists the Steam features your store page claims (Steam Cloud, PvP, online co-op, split screen) and the languages promised, and has a field for test accounts if multiplayer needs special access before release. Game Developer adds that Next Fest submissions roughly doubled their previous high.
blocks.why: Release dates on Steam now need about three weeks of slack for review, and a failed check costs another full wait. Running Valve's own checklist before you press submit is the cheapest way to avoid that.
blocks.forYou: Put a 15 business day review buffer in the action RPG's release plan, and make sure every feature on its store page (co-op, controller support, languages) is reachable in the first minutes of the build.

sources.label: Valve: Updates to the pre-release review process

Kotaku: devs forced to delay their games on Steam

blocks.title: What Steam now checks before it reviews your build
blocks.gist: Valve added five items to the checklist every game must clear before review. Each one targets a basic failure that sends games back into the queue.
blocks.intro: The new items from Valve's November 3 post, in the order to do them. They show up in the release checklist on your app's Steamworks page.

steps.title: Play it through Steam for 5 minutes
steps.text: Press the green Play button in the Steam client, not your executable. Any team member's playtime counts if it is from the last 7 days or since the last build. It catches wrong launch options and missing depots.

steps.title: Declare redistributables
steps.text: Tell Steam which shared libraries to install (DirectX, Visual C++, .NET and so on), or state that the game needs none.

steps.title: Finish the achievements
steps.text: Steam now flags missing names, missing icons and duplicate names in your achievement setup.

steps.title: Write one cloud save
steps.text: If the page lists Steam Cloud, someone in your partner group must write a save to it, and developer-only sync mode must be switched off.

steps.title: Label five gameplay screenshots
steps.text: Screenshots now carry categories (gameplay, menus, concept art, cinematics). At least five must be gameplay, and none may carry marketing copy.

terms.def: The sets of files Steam downloads for a game, for example one per platform or per add-on.

blocks.why: Each item matches a reason Valve says games fail and get re-reviewed, so clearing them up front is the most direct way to stay out of the 12 day queue twice.
blocks.forYou: Add these five checks to the release checklist in the RPG repo, and keep the Steam Cloud save path test as an automated step.

sources.label: Valve: Updates to the pre-release review process

blocks.title: Sale banners leave the top of Steam pages
blocks.gist: Steam no longer puts a sale event banner across the top of a game's store page. Events now sit in a new section lower down that shows each player the games from that sale it thinks they will like.
body: Valve said on November 4 that games in many events at once ended up with a banner for almost every visitor, which pushed the game's own information down. The banners are gone; a personalized event section now sits beside the "More like this" carousel.
When a game is in several events, Steam shows the one with the most games it recommends to that player. The section appears only during the first two weeks of an event.
points: Applies to publisher sales, themed and regional sales, and showcase events.
Traffic from it shows in Steamworks under "More from sale events".

image.alt: A Steam store page section titled "Guns of Eschaton is part of an event": the gamescom asia event banner on the left and three games "Recommended for you from this event" on the right.

blocks.why: Joining a themed sale now buys a slot in a recommendation shelf rather than a banner on your own page, so its value depends on overlap with the other games in that event.
blocks.forYou: When picking themed sales for the RPG, prefer events full of similar action RPGs: the section only surfaces games the player is likely to want.

blocks.title: Linked Discord players stay longer, says Discord
blocks.gist: Discord says players who link their game account to Discord keep playing noticeably longer. The numbers are Discord's own, from its partners.

stats.label: median lift in day-28 retention for linked players (vendor data)
of Marvel Rivals pilot purchases were gifts

body: Discord's Anthony Tesija told PocketGamer.biz linked players also open the game on 25% more days. Linkers are likely the most engaged players already, so treat this as an upper bound.

blocks.title: Agents lose about 12 points when you make them juggle tasks
blocks.gist: Researchers gave coding agents one task, then the same task with four other half-finished jobs mixed into the session. Every agent solved fewer, and a simple per-task memory got most of the loss back.
blocks.intro: Points of solve rate lost on the same 200 Python tasks when they are interleaved with other unfinished tasks, by agent and model (higher is worse).
blocks.note: Claude Code fell from 53.5% to 41.5%. Interruptions from a distant part of the repo hurt more (14.9 points on average) than nearby ones (8.1). Python only.

terms.def: The share of tasks where the agent's final change passes the hidden tests.

deep: Switch-SWE (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Tongji University) builds 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories. Each runs once alone and once with four other unfinished tasks from the same repository interleaved; only the final patch for the focus task is scored. Across seven agent and model pairs the gap averaged 11.5 points (6.0 to 15.0), and switched sessions also used more tokens and tool calls.

Their Resumption Context Manager routes each turn to its task's history and keeps a per-task state memory. On OpenCode it recovered 5.5 to 15.5 points; it was tested only there, with two models. Code is on GitHub.
blocks.why: Sessions that carry several unfinished jobs cost more and solve less. One task per session, with a short state note to resume from, is cheap insurance.
blocks.forYou: Stop resuming one long Claude Code session across plugin tasks: one worktree and one session per task, each with its own state file.

blocks.title: Conductor joins Meta and shuts its app down
blocks.gist: Conductor, a Mac app for running several coding agents side by side, is joining Meta. Its cloud service closes this month and the desktop app winds down early next year, so users need to export their work.
blocks.intro: The dates from Conductor's announcement. Active subscribers are refunded.

events.text: No new sign-ups or downloads. Pro users keep pro features free.
Conductor Cloud turns read-only: old chats readable and exportable, no new messages.
Cloud shuts down and deletion of cloud data begins. Export before this: Settings, Account, Export data.
The local app stops; until then it still gets new models and critical fixes.

terms.def: A second working folder for the same git repository, so two agents can edit separate branches at once.

blocks.why: Tools that orchestrate your agents hold your session history. Keep that history in files you own, such as plain git worktrees and notes, so a shutdown costs an afternoon, not your context.

blocks.title: Proving which model answered you, at 70 times the cost
blocks.gist: Anthropic released a prototype that lets an AI provider prove a reply came from a specific model, which anyone can check without seeing the model. It is far too slow for everyday use.

stats.label: GPU time of normal serving, for the prover
to verify one 1,024-token reply on a CPU

body: Tested on a 400B open model. It handles only short, deterministic replies, and the code is open source under Apache 2.0.

terms.def: A way to prove a statement is true without revealing the secret behind it, here the model's weights.

deep: FlashProve, from Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, uses a zero-knowledge proof (a zkSNARK) against a public commitment to the weights. On Llama 4 Maverick at 4-bit it proves about 110 tokens a second on one H100; proofs are about 18.8 MB per 1,024-token window; setup takes about 39 minutes and the commitment covers about 16 million requests. Limits: integer weights, greedy decoding, 1,024-token context, mixture-of-experts models only.
blocks.why: If you pay for a specific model through a reseller, today you have to trust them. This is the first practical-looking path to checking.

blocks.title: A 65B open model claims the top coding score
blocks.gist: A small company released an open-weight coding model of 65 billion parameters that, on its own test run, scores slightly above open models eight to fifteen times its size. Nobody has checked the result independently yet.
blocks.intro: Terminal-Bench 2.1 scores as published by Ricursive on November 4, with total parameter counts. All figures are vendor-reported.
blocks.note: Ricursive says the whole project cost about $32 million, with 70 times fewer reinforcement learning runs than Beam. The licence is not stated on the launch page.

terms.def: A model whose trained parameters are published, so anyone can download and run it.
A benchmark where an agent completes real tasks in a command-line environment.

deep: Ripple-65B is a dense model (every parameter is used for every token), 80 layers deep, pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with context up to 1 million tokens. It is on Hugging Face and served by Together AI, GMI Cloud and OpenRouter. The maker says it runs on an NVIDIA DGX Spark class machine but gives no setup.

The same week Moonshot published the weights of Kimi K3.1 Pro, a 2.8 trillion parameter mixture-of-experts model with 104B active, under a custom licence. Its vendor scores use different benchmark versions, so they cannot be placed on this chart.
blocks.why: A dense model this size fits on one large workstation, which would make a strong agent model cheap to run privately. Wait for independent runs before switching.
blocks.forYou: Worth one OpenRouter trial on a real plugin task once a third party confirms the score; read the licence first.

blocks.title: Let Postgres move the big column out, or move it yourself
blocks.gist: Postgres can store large text or JSON values in a side table so the main table stays small. A test on 100,000 rows shows how much faster ordinary queries run when it does, and how to get the same win on purpose.
blocks.background: TOAST is how Postgres (and so Supabase) handles big values: above about 2 KB it compresses them and moves them to a hidden side table, leaving a pointer in the row.
blocks.intro: Shaun Thomas (pgEdge) loaded 100,000 rows with one JSON column of up to 1,000 fields, once with default storage (big values moved out) and once forced to stay inline. Single runs, hardware not stated.

rows.aspect: Read one field from every JSON value

blocks.verdict: Moving big values out speeds up everything that does not read them, and slightly slows the queries that do. Splitting the column into its own table took the main table to about 5 MB.

terms.def: The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique: Postgres's way of compressing large values and storing them outside the main table.
A fast compression method Postgres 14 and later can use instead of its older default, pglz.

deep: The fix in the post: create a narrow table and a separate table holding the id and the big column, copy the data, swap names, then recreate the old shape as a view with a LEFT JOIN. Queries that never touch the big column get the join removed by the planner; a primary key lookup used 3 buffer hits.

Set COMPRESSION lz4 on the column (or default_toast_compression). On 100,000 rows of 90,000-character values, inserts took 1.8 s with lz4 against 52.2 s with pglz; reading them back was about 20% slower. In the production case behind the post, the main table was over 1 GB and the total with its side table over 20 GB.
blocks.why: Any table with a large JSON or text column that apps read with SELECT * is a candidate. The split-plus-view trick keeps existing queries working.
blocks.forYou: Check the SaaS tables with JSON payload columns on Supabase: compare main table size against total size, and try the split-plus-view on the largest.

blocks.title: Safari may darken your light site for you
blocks.gist: A new Safari beta can turn light websites dark on its own when the user's system is in dark mode. One line of CSS or HTML tells it whether your site handles dark mode itself.
blocks.intro: From WebKit's November 3 post on Safari 27.3 beta. The same values work in a color-scheme meta tag; declare them in HTML or CSS, not from JavaScript.
explain: The adaptation inverts lightness but keeps hue, aims for 4.5:1 text contrast, and leaves canvas content and most bitmap images alone. It can switch off some masks and mix-blend-mode effects on changed elements.
The `only` keyword was not yet supported in beta 1, so test in the beta before relying on it.
blocks.why: Pages with blend modes, masks or brand colors may look wrong without your consent. Browser games drawn on a canvas are untouched, but their HTML menus are not.
blocks.forYou: Add the color-scheme meta to the SaaS apps and the web game shells, and check the web game's HTML menus in the Safari beta.

blocks.title: Cloudflare D1 now rejects results over 50 MB
blocks.gist: Since November 4, Cloudflare's D1 database refuses any query whose result is larger than 50 MB. Apps that load whole tables in one go will start getting errors.

stats.label: largest query result D1 will return

body: The error reads "D1 query result exceeded the maximum response size limit of 50 MB". Cloudflare's advice: select only the columns you need instead of `SELECT *`, and page through large results with LIMIT and OFFSET.
Import and export through the REST API are exempt.

terms.def: Cloudflare's hosted SQLite database for apps running on its Workers platform.

blocks.why: A query that worked last week can fail today once a table grows past the cap, so search your code for unbounded selects now.
blocks.forYou: Grep any Workers projects for SELECT * against D1 and add LIMIT to the admin and export routes.

sources.label: Cloudflare changelog: D1 query result size limit

learn.question: What is an agent's context, and why does a full one hurt?
learn.answer: Context is everything a model can see at once while it works: instructions, files it read, tool output and the conversation so far. It has a size limit, and as it fills, each new step gets slower, costlier and easier to get wrong.
learn.analogy: A desk: you can only work with the papers on it. Pile on notes from five unrelated jobs and you spend your time hunting for the right sheet.
body: A coding agent re-reads its whole context on every step. Each file it opens and each command's output stays there, so a long session grows until it hits the model's limit, measured in tokens (pieces of words).

Two of today's studies point the same way. In Switch-SWE, mixing other unfinished tasks into a session cost agents up to 15 points. In NVIDIA's "You don't need long context", summarizing the history when it got long (compaction) changed accuracy by a few points either way while cutting estimated cost two to nine times.
The practical habits: one task per session, big logs kept as files the agent can search instead of pasted in, and a short written state to carry over when you start fresh.

diagram.caption: Everything an agent sees piles into one window; keeping it short is most of the craft.

Replacing a long conversation history with a short summary so the agent can keep going.

tryThis.title: Give each unfinished task its own session and a state note
tryThis.gist: You find out whether splitting juggled work into one-task sessions, each resumed from a short note, makes your agent pick up faster and use less context.
tryThis.needs: A repository with two or more unfinished tasks and a coding agent such as Claude Code.

steps.title: Write one note per task
steps.text: For each unfinished task, create a small file such as tasks/<name>.md with three parts: the requirement, what is done, and the next step. This is the per-task state memory Switch-SWE used.

steps.title: Open a fresh session per task
steps.text: Start a new session (or a new git worktree) for one task only, and tell the agent to read that task's note and nothing about the others.

steps.title: Update the note before you stop
steps.text: At the end of the session, ask the agent to rewrite the note: what changed, what is left, the exact next step.

steps.title: Compare with your old way
steps.text: Resume the second task the old way, in your long mixed session, and note how much context is in use and whether the agent's first action is the right next step.

code.code:
# Task: <name>
## Requirement
<what must be true when done>
## Done so far
- <change, file>
## Next step
<one concrete action>

tryThis.check: In the fresh session the context in use at the start is far smaller (in Claude Code, /context shows it), and the agent's first move is the next step from the note rather than re-reading the repository.

terms.def: A second working folder for the same git repository, so separate tasks keep separate files.

tryThis.forYou: Try it on the two plugin tasks that keep sharing one long session; keep the notes in each plugin repo's tasks folder.

sparks.title: Co-op added to 1990's Wing Commander after a decade of reverse engineering
sparks.signal: 140 points on Show HN on November 4; first memory dumps date from October 2015.
sparks.hook: Two players fly as wingmates in a browser build of DOSBox, using their own copy of the game. The developers found ship positions by diffing memory while moving one control at a time, then hooked the main loop.
sparks.borrow: The snapshot-diff trick to find game state, and the small Go lobby that pairs browsers by room code over WebRTC, are both reusable for browser multiplayer.

image.alt: Two Wing Commander cockpits side by side, each showing a wingman's chat line, one per player.

sparks.title: Kickturn: a 3D skate game for Playdate, written and judged by agents
sparks.signal: 289 commits in three days for 1-BIT JAM 15, from 17 to 30 frames a second measured on the device; small social reach so far.
sparks.hook: Builder agents wrote it while separate read-only judge agents scored each round, and the technical score was capped until it ran on real hardware.
sparks.borrow: A replay gate: 57 recorded scenarios run headless and 251 key frames are diffed on every change, so an agent cannot quietly break another part of the game.

image.alt: Chart "Three days, 289 commits": 3 commits on day one, 133 in rounds 1 to 9 with agents judging, 153 in round 10 when the renderer moved to C, reaching 30 fps.

sparks.forYou: Borrow the replay gate for the plugin test maps: record inputs, dump state hashes, fail the agent's commit on any diff.

sparks.title: Agents play League of Legends, and thinking longer makes them worse
sparks.signal: 6 upvotes on Hugging Face papers; the best agent completed a quarter of 36 champion tasks.
sparks.hook: The game does not pause while the model thinks, so a click chosen from an old screenshot lands on a scene that has moved on.
sparks.borrow: For any real-time game bot or playtest agent, budget for latency: more reasoning bought no gain here, and fewer, faster decisions did better.

image.alt: Figure: in a paused game the scene is unchanged between observing and acting; in LOLPlay ten seconds pass, health drops from 648 to 333 and the planned click lands in the wrong place.

sparks.title: Fold: drag a sheet of jelly plastic, day one of mrdoob's agentic Codevember
sparks.signal: 448 points and 113 comments on Hacker News on November 4.
sparks.hook: The three.js creator is building one interactive piece a day in November with coding agents, from a one-word prompt list. Day one is a thick, refractive cloth you can grab and fling.
sparks.borrow: The source is public: a CPU cloth simulation feeding a fixed-topology mesh rendered with three.js's WebGPU renderer, with ambient occlusion as post-processing. A commenter found it fails on Firefox Mobile, so plan a fallback.
sparks.forYou: Read 01/main.js for the WebGPU and TSL setup before the next browser game's renderer pass.

sparks.title: Uncracked City: question suspects who lie, in real cities
sparks.signal: 123 points and 66 comments on Show HN on November 3.
sparks.hook: Cases are set in real public places from Lisbon to Seoul; you catch a lie by setting a clue against a statement, typing or speaking in six languages.
sparks.borrow: The solo founder says a model must solve every generated case before it goes live: an automated solvability check for any generated puzzle or quest.

sparks.title: Declarative dragging: describe where things can go, get drag and drop for free
sparks.signal: UIST 2026 best paper, shared on lobste.rs this week; a niche pick so far.
sparks.hook: Instead of writing drag handlers, you list the states a drag can lead to; the library renders each one, sees where the item lands, and builds snapping drop zones from that.
sparks.borrow: Inventory grids, card piles and node editors are all "which states can this lead to" problems. The library, dragology, is on npm.

image.alt: Diagram: a render function maps state to view; when a drag starts, possible target states are computed and rendered; where the dragged element lands in each becomes a drop zone.

lab.title: You don't need long context
lab.headline: Summarize the history early and agents cost two to nine times less
lab.authors: Peter Belcak, Saurav Muralidharan, Jindong Jiang, et al. (NVIDIA Research)
lab.problem: Each new token costs more to generate the longer the context already is, and agents pay that premium for the whole session.
lab.idea: Test three habits on 13 benchmarks: compact the history when it nears a threshold; keep long inputs as files the agent searches with shell tools instead of loading them; or give every action its own context, carrying only a compact state forward.
lab.result: With Claude Opus 4.5, compaction moved accuracy between -3.7 and +5.6 points while estimated cost fell 2.2 to 8.8 times. Reading long inputs as files cut cost 6.5 to 54.6 times. One action per context lifted Terminal-Bench from 47.2% to 51.8% on Opus but lowered GPT 5.6 Sol, and costs are estimated, not billed.
lab.useIt: Compact earlier rather than riding the window to its limit, keep big logs and docs as files for the agent to search, and for long unattended jobs, split work into short sessions that hand over a state file.

image.alt: Three charts against context length up to 256K tokens for five open models: latency per token rises, decode speed falls, and memory use climbs toward the device limit.

lab.forYou: Lower the auto-compact point on the long Radar and plugin runs and keep build logs on disk for grep; compare token use over a week.

lab.title: Code Understanding is a Bottleneck for Coding Agents
lab.headline: Agents fail at reading code, not at editing it
lab.authors: Nishant Balepur, Kiran Tomlinson, Tobias Schnabel (Microsoft Research)
lab.problem: How hard a coding task is gets judged by how many lines change, which says little about why agents fail.
lab.idea: CABRA generates 6,840 synthetic tasks by transforming call graphs, and scales difficulty along four axes: following calls, searching, resolving what runs at runtime, and following instructions.
lab.result: Agents stay near perfect on large tasks a bare model fails, because they offload to search tools. How many read and analysis tool calls an agent makes predicts its SWE-bench Verified accuracy better than lines edited does. Accuracy finally falls when agents must compare how two similar classes diverge.
lab.useIt: Give agents fast search and a map of the codebase, and review closely any change that depends on how two near-identical classes differ.

image.alt: Figure: a task to extract logically equivalent code from two classes; agent accuracy falling as total lines of code grow from 5 to 200; and analysis tool calls rising sharply with code size.

lab.forYou: The UE plugins have many near-identical component classes; keep a symbol map in CLAUDE.md and review diffs that touch sibling classes by hand.

lab.title: GameVerse: A Minute-Scale Gameplay Dataset for Long-Horizon Interactive World Modeling
lab.headline: 1,655 hours of game footage to keep AI-generated worlds coherent longer
lab.authors: Kang He, Wenshuo Peng, Chuanhao Li, et al. (Alaya Lab, Shanghai Innovation Institute, Wuhan University, Tsinghua University)
lab.problem: Playable world models drift and lose consistency after about a minute, partly because they are trained on short clips.
lab.idea: Cut 11,002 YouTube gameplay videos from over 110 games into 69,700 clips, most of them two continuous minutes, with camera paths and four levels of captions from scene to player action.
lab.result: Fine-tuning HY-World 1.5 on it raised a 3D consistency score from 66.94 to 73.42, and the time before the picture drifts past a similarity threshold rose from 30.4 to 37.9 seconds. Tests stop at 60 seconds.
lab.useIt: A guide to where playable world models are heading and a data recipe for fine-tuning one; the footage comes from YouTube, so check rights before any commercial use.

image.alt: Figure: a gameplay video cut into scene clips, a five-step quality pipeline, two-minute clips with camera trajectory and layered captions, and charts of clip length, game genres and player actions.
